source.version_note: Cognitive Science 44(7), e12872; online 6 July 2020 and July 2020 issue. Supplied download date/watermark is not the publication date and is not reproduced.
source.verification_method: All twelve supplied pages, the three-panel mind-perception figure, three stimulus images and complete bibliography read. Publisher/Crossref verify identity and online/issue dates. MIT Press book metadata verifies editor names only. The indexed DOCX supplement could not be retrieved; no appendix, video, participant data, analysis code or computational reproduction claimed.

citation.title: Robots as Malevolent Moral Agents: Harmful Behavior Results in Dehumanization, Not Anthropomorphism

reading.source_scope_note: Three vignette experiments test human attributions of mind to harmful or helpful robotic agents, with a human-agent comparison in E3. These are observer judgments of described/rendered behavior and perceived victim suffering, not actual robot intentions, human injury, objective pain or a universal dehumanization mechanism.
access_limits: All main text, notes, bibliography, Figure 1’s three panels and Figure 2’s three images were read. Figure 1 pools agent types in E3 rather than presenting robot-specific bars.

The publisher index identifies cogs12872-sup-0001-Supinfo.docx, approximately 25.9 KB, covering E1 vignettes and E2–3 intentional-stance results. The attempted Wiley supplement download returned HTTP 403 and cached article views omitted a working supplement link. No supplementary text, file checksum or complete item wording was obtained.

No animation viewed, raw participant file downloaded, original statistical code executed, preregistration independently located or original model reproduced. Absence of an obtained registration is not proof that one does not exist.

Prior moral-typecasting/dehumanization experiments, robotics books, Asimov editions and original empathy instruments were not independently fully read. MIT Press metadata supplies editor identity only; an unrelated result from a broad chapter-title query was not substituted as the cited source.

study.samples: E1 N 125, E2 N 112 and E3 N 129: 366 study participations, not independently verified unique people. Means ages are approximately 33.6, 33.8 and 34.2; sample recruitment and full exclusion details are not specified in the main text. Targets from conventional medium-effect power analyses do not establish sensitivity to small or interaction effects.
study.e1_design: Random assignment crosses an attack versus failure-to-support scene with mechanistic versus mentalistic text, four groups. Both harmful outcomes occur; the manipulations bundle action/omission and narrative content rather than isolating intention with identical behavior. The perceived-intent check is nonsignificant, p .228, with both means below the scale midpoint.
study.e1_measures: Seven experience items, seven agency items and two consciousness items are rated on 1–7 scales; moral evaluation and perceived intentionality are separate questions. Experience items include personality and desire alongside feelings and hunger, while agency includes moral understanding and communication. These are selected scale contents, not pure biological capacities or proof of a universal two-factor structure.
study.e1_results: Multivariate assigned-scene effect F(3,119) 4.66, p .004; agency F(1,121) 6.73, p .011 and consciousness F 4.74, p .031, while experience F .74, p .392 is nonsignificant. Stance main effect is nonsignificant. A reported difference between scenes is not a successful clean manipulation of subjectively perceived intention, and null wording effects do not establish equivalence.
study.e2_design: Three static scenes show a robot holding a club to attack, stretching its arms toward a falling man or remaining unresponsive. Weapon presence, facial expression, action and intention cues differ. The authors explicitly recognize possible weapon salience and fearful-expression confounds but do not measure attention or test those mediators.
study.e2_results: Overall mind MANOVA has p .070. Experience univariate F(2,109) 3.93, p .022; benevolent mean 3.39 exceeds malevolent 2.67 and unresponsive 2.42. Agency and consciousness contrasts are nonsignificant. Thus the harmful robot is not shown to be lower than the unresponsive control on every mind measure; increased attribution to the helping image is another possible framing.
study.e2_activity: The attacking robot is rated more vigorous/active than the other robots. Observable activity is not interchangeable with inferred planning or self-control. No measured weapon-focus mechanism establishes why agency results differ by format. Moral evaluation df 108 versus usual 109 suggests one missing rating or another analysis difference, not a safely guessed exclusion.
study.e3_design: Randomly selected animations cross human versus robot agent and kicking versus approaching/kneeling when an older man falls. There is no unresponsive/accidental control in E3. Same named action and rendered outcome are not independent measurements of equal actual injury or medical severity.
study.e3_mind: Agent main effect is strongest for experience, human 5.32 versus robot 2.91. Agency and consciousness source differences are nonsignificant. Assigned behavior has significant main effects on all three mind scales; the formal multivariate agent × behavior interaction is nonsignificant, F(3,123) .46, p .714. These are pooled main effects; lack of interaction does not prove identical human and robot responses or establish each unreported conditional contrast.
study.e3_patient: Exploratory perceived-suffering ratings average 6.09 with human agents versus 5.68 with robots, source main effect F(1,125) 5.96, p .016. Harm versus help also differs. The source main effect averages over both behavior conditions; a harm-only contrast or source × behavior interaction is not reported. State-empathy source/behavior effects are nonsignificant with trait concern controlled. Lower inferred suffering is not reduced actual pain, lower capacity to feel or diminished rights.
study.uncanniness: The paragraph placed before E3 uses human and robot comparisons and df 125, matching the E3 design/sample rather than robot-only E2 N 112. Its unease ratings do not trace a nonlinear appearance continuum and hence do not independently establish an uncanny-valley curve. Exact experiment placement still requires the original output.
study.interpretation: The authors favor reduced mind attribution over the proposed increase for harmful agents, but outcomes differ by measure, scenario and experiment. E1’s intention check, E2’s image confounds and E3’s pooled effects constrain a clean mechanism claim. Denying real people humanity and attributing fewer mental capacities to a robot are not automatically the same process.
study.cross_study: The 2026 Augustine/Eyssel experiments use these care/harm materials but report different human/robot mind patterns and no significant robot behavior contrasts. They are not an exact protocol replication or proof that either source is false; their mixed outcomes constrain a universal robot-dehumanization claim.

summary: Enrich existing mind-attribution and dehumanization records with this original three-experiment study and the later contrasting evidence. Keep exploratory suffering judgments, scene differences and measured mechanisms separate. No new established behavior name is supplied by the proposed inversion of harm-made mind, so no row is added.

findings.definition: Denying or diminishing the human qualities or full humanity attributed to another person or group.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: a significantly decreased attribution of mind compared to benevolent

findings.evidence_scope: The paper interprets lower mind ratings after harmful versus helpful scenes using dehumanization theory. E3 includes human and robot agents, but the significant behavior effect is pooled and the formal multivariate source interaction is null. This is an attribution pattern with mixed measures, not a universal process.
findings.boundary: The existing definition concerns denied humanity of people or groups. Lower robot mind attribution is an analogue and does not alone meet that definition, nor identify denial of human nature versus human uniqueness. Criticism of a harmful act is not automatically dehumanization.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: intentionally harmful agents were perceived to possess less agency

findings.evidence_scope: Assigned harmful-scene variants differ on attributed planning/control-related capacities in E1; E3 also shows a pooled behavior effect, whereas E2 agency is nonsignificant. E1 perceived-intent manipulation check fails to distinguish the scenes significantly.
findings.boundary: Assigned scene, perceived intention, activity, agency and actual intent differ. Do not call an unsuccessful subjective-intent check successful, infer absence from a null or treat a pooled E3 effect as every agent-specific contrast.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: participants attributed more capacity for experience to the benevolent robot

findings.evidence_scope: The helping robot’s image receives higher experience ratings than attacking or unresponsive images in E2; E1 experience is nonsignificant. E3 shows human/robot and pooled behavior differences, with no significant multivariate interaction.
findings.boundary: Weapon and facial-expression differences are not isolated mediators. An observer’s lower suffering estimate for a human victim does not measure the victim’s capacity for experience, actual pain or moral worth.

findings.definition: Interpreting and predicting an agent's behavior by treating it as guided by beliefs, desires or intentions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: both its internal states and actions (mentalistic stance)

findings.evidence_scope: E1 explicitly varies mentalistic versus action-focused wording, while the reported stance main effect is nonsignificant. Additional perceived-stance results are referred to an unavailable supplement.
findings.boundary: A narrative describing beliefs or desires is not proof of actual consciousness or a measured increase in intentional-stance adoption. No supplement results are claimed read, and the null wording effect does not establish equivalence.

findings.definition: Increased attribution of mental capacities to an entity when it is perceived as harmed or victimized.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: an inversion of the original harm-made mind effect

findings.evidence_scope: The authors speculate that lower perceived suffering with robot agents could invert harm-made mind. Their outcome is an exploratory suffering estimate rather than the victim’s newly attributed mental capacity, and the source main effect pools harm/help scenes.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only hypothesis, not a newly established opposite behavior or direct demonstration of victim mind denial. Do not infer actual reduced suffering, discount a complaint or adjust care based on perpetrator type.

findings.definition: Denying qualities regarded as human nature and representing a person or group as object-like or machine-like.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add this original study’s conditional evidence and contrasting results to an existing construct; an exploratory interpretation is not automatically another named behavior.

evidence.quote: lesser perceived suffering extends to decreased attributions of the capacity

findings.evidence_scope: The paper explicitly leaves open whether perceived-suffering differences extend to ratings of capacity for pain or experience. It does not separately test the human-nature denial criteria of mechanistic dehumanization.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only distinction. A lower situational suffering estimate or robot attribution is not sufficient evidence of representing a real human as machine-like, and human rights cannot depend on observers’ mental-capacity ratings.

public_supplement.reading: Not retrieved or read; HTTP 403. Indexed filename/description is metadata only. No text, checksum, implied file identity or full-supplement credit.

source_corrections.reported: Robot Ethics editors are written L. Patrick and A. Keith alongside G. A. Bekey.
source_corrections.correction: Use Patrick Lin, Keith Abney and George A. Bekey, verified on the MIT Press book page. Preserve the chapter/year context; 2011 ebook and 2014 paperback dates do not by themselves invalidate a 2012 volume citation.
source_corrections.scope: Editor identity only; no full book or chapter reading credit.

source_corrections.reported: F(2,109) 3.93 is paired with partial eta-squared .08.
source_corrections.correction: Conditional on the printed F and degrees of freedom, F×df1/(F×df1+df2) gives approximately .0673, rounding to .07. Flag the mismatch with .08 without changing the observed F, p value or source data.
source_corrections.scope: Algebraic consistency check of the printed test, not an original-model reproduction.

source_corrections.reported: The source main effect is interpreted as identical harm causing less suffering when a robot inflicts it.
source_corrections.correction: State that these are observer ratings and that the reported agent contrast averages harmful and helpful conditions. A harm-only effect and a difference between behavior-specific effects require their own direct contrasts. Actual injury and pain were not measured.
source_corrections.scope: Estimand and outcome qualification; not a guessed unreported p value.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The paragraph appears in E2 results but contains human/robot cells and df 125. E2 has robot-only N 112, while E3 has that factorial design and N 129. It appears misplaced, but original output is needed to authenticate its correct experiment label; do not invent an extra E2 human sample.

The MANOVA description mentions Bonferroni correction, but the scope of the correction across outcomes and follow-ups is unclear. Printed univariate p values correspond to their F tests. Do not assert all tests passed a newly imposed correction or silently recategorize the authors’ procedure.
Moral evaluation has residual df 108 while other E2 tests have 109. A missing item could explain this, but complete data and preprocessing were not obtained; no specific exclusion is invented.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Conditional robot effects and later contrast
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: E3 mind and suffering main effects are pooled. The later Augustine/Eyssel source reports different conditional patterns, but protocols and scales differ. No formal cross-study interaction, equivalence result or meta-analysis was performed.

methodological_limits: 366 retained study participations provide observer ratings of vignettes, not natural robot encounters or an independent census. Recruitment, exclusions and cross-study overlap cannot be reconstructed from the main paper.

The E1 scene manipulation does not significantly shift reported intentionality; attack versus omission, outcomes and narrative cues differ. E2 weapon presence and expression confounds are acknowledged but not tested as mechanisms.

Mind measures are selected items with their own content and reliability, not direct access to real robot or human subjective states. Agency, observable activity, intentionality, emotion and consciousness are distinct.
E2’s multivariate p .070 and its narrower experience result must both be retained. A harmful agent is not consistently lower on all outcomes or than every control. Nulls do not establish equality.

E3 reports a genuine null multivariate source × behavior interaction and pooled main effects. Neither pooled significance nor a null interaction establishes equal conditional effects or validates all subgroup claims.
Perceived suffering, empathic concern and actual pain are separate endpoints. No injury or legitimate care entitlement can be discounted because a machine rather than a person caused an event.

Trait concern is a covariate in reported exploratory analyses; adjusting for it does not establish a unique causal path. No victim-capacity or mediation test demonstrates an inverse harm-made-mind mechanism.

Later contrasting results constrain universality without proving misconduct or a definitive failed replication. An inaccessible supplement and lack of source output prevent complete reproducibility, not all interpretation.
No new behavior name is invented for a speculative interpretation, and no metadata-only book check receives full-source credit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Being harmed as a target and causing harm as an agent are different roles. Moral evaluation, experience ratings and actual mentality must remain separate, and a source’s named theory need not uniquely explain the result.
Aggregate or selected-item mind dimensions depend on the task and instrument. A difference in a broad mind score does not establish a universal latent architecture or actual sentience.

The later care/harm experiments explicitly use this source’s materials and report different robot-specific mind results. Preserve both papers and their actual formal interaction evidence rather than count them as uniform confirmation.

deferred.term: Inverse harm-made mind as a new established behavior
deferred.reason: The authors explicitly call the interpretation speculative. Perceived suffering is not the victim’s attributed capacity, and the reported source main effect pools harm and help scenes.

deferred.term: Weapon focus as a newly demonstrated mechanism here
deferred.reason: Weapon salience is an explanation for a confounded stimulus contrast; attention was not measured or independently manipulated. The original cited weapon-focus study was not read in full.

deferred.term: Robot dehumanization as another independent synonym row
deferred.reason: Retain the existing human concept and mark the robot extension as an analogy, with mind-attribution outcomes stored in the existing agency/experience entries.

limitations: No new entry. Existing stable IDs and eleven categories preserved; no forced citation quota, invented annual totals, automatic ethical/harm edges or full-paper Markdown transcription.
